records.title: Sex steroids in animals absent gonads: A case series.
records.abstract: Identifying possible sources of sex steroids is challenging in animals exhibiting apparent responses in reproductive tissues but presenting with a history of having been neutered. Sex steroids, typically secreted by the gonads, also induce responses in non-reproductive tissues including the skin or brain, sometimes affecting behaviors. The analysis of hormones has become a mainstay of diagnostic endocrinology in small and large animal practice. The repertoire of those with reproductive relevance has expanded significantly with specific immunoassays detecting anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) from either ovarian granulosa or testicular Sertoli cells. This has proven to be extremely useful differentiating neutered animals from those that are not. When AMH is undetectable, indicating neutered status, the possibility of sex steroid secretion by non-gonadal, pathological tissue, or other exogenous sources becomes very real. Reported gonadal status (as stated by owners) is not always reliable given that changes of ownership are common, and neutering is not always complete, complicating initial diagnosis. The cases reported here include several that are unique in either their presentation, diagnostic approach or likely etiologic origin. All were submitted primarily for an assessment of their gonadal status. Collectively, they illustrate, with unusual insight, the utility of AMH as a gonadal biomarker, while obviating the complexity of interpretation of reproductive hormone analyses in supposedly gonadectomized cats, horses and dogs manifesting a variety of apparent, reproductive conditions and pathologies.

records.title: Rare Feline Gingival Extramedullary Plasmacytoma: Clinical Application of Electrochemotherapy for Local Control.
records.abstract: Feline extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP) is an uncommon plasma cell neoplasm typically regarded as biologically benign; however, its clinical behaviour may be heterogeneous. This case report describes an aggressive gingival EMP in a 14-year-old neutered male Turkish Angora cat, characterised by alveolar bone lysis and cytologically confirmed regional lymph node metastasis in the absence of systemic features consistent with multiple myeloma. Histopathological examination revealed an infiltrative round cell neoplasm with high mitotic index, and strong diffuse MUM-1 immunoreactivity confirmed the diagnosis. As complete surgical excision was declined, and tumour regrowth occurred after repeated radiation therapy, electrochemotherapy (ECT) was selected for local tumour control. Bleomycin (15,000 IU/m 2  IV) was administered before pulse delivery, and three ECT sessions were performed at weekly intervals. The tumour volume decreased by more than 70%, which was consistent with a partial response, and only mild self-limiting local adverse effects were observed. No systemic toxicity was observed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report describing the use of ECT for feline gingival EMP. This case highlights the potential biological heterogeneity of feline EMP and suggests that ECT may provide short-term local tumour reduction and palliation when complete surgical excision is not feasible.

records.title: Computed Tomographic Findings of Hepatic Rupture Associated With Amyloidosis in a Young Siamese Cat.
records.journal: Veterinary radiology & ultrasound : the official journal of the American College of Veterinary Radiology and the International Veterinary Radiology Association
records.abstract: A 3-year-old neutered male Siamese cat with chronic anorexia showed anemia and elevated liver enzyme levels. Ultrasonography disclosed multiple diffusely heterogeneous hepatic lesions and peritoneal effusion, which was identified as hemoabdomen upon fluid analysis. Computed tomography showed finger-like hypoattenuation extending from the left hepatic margin with focal margin loss in the delayed phase, suggesting hepatic rupture. Infiltrative hepatic diseases were considered, and amyloidosis was the top differential diagnosis given the patient's young age, breed predisposition, and suspected hepatic rupture. Blood oozing was confirmed via laparotomy, and Congo red staining established hepatic amyloidosis, though amyloid typing was not pursued.

records.title: Spontaneous Reduction in Mitral Valve Regurgitation in Three Dogs With Severe Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease: An Unusual Case Report.
records.abstract: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), the most common heart disease in small-breed dogs, is characterized by mitral regurgitation (MR) resulting from valvular degeneration, which may progress to left-sided heart failure. This report describes the cases of three dogs with severe MMVD (American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine Stages C or D) who exhibited an unexpected spontaneous reduction in MR despite continued valve degeneration. Three dogs initially presented with symptoms of heart failure and left atrial and ventricular enlargement. Standard treatment, including diuretics, improved their conditions; however, further monitoring revealed that the coaptation gap decreased due to mitral valve thickening, leading to a reduction in MR. This was accompanied by a significant decrease in heart size. As a result, diuretics were discontinued, and all dogs were successfully managed with pimobendan alone. To our knowledge, this is the first report of spontaneous MR reduction in MMVD, where coaptation gap narrowing played a role in clinical improvement. These cases may broaden the current understanding of MMVD progression, suggesting that, in rare instances, changes in cardiac remodelling and clinical status can occur. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms.

records.title: Left Medial Liver Lobe Torsion Associated With Hepatocellular Carcinoma in a Pembroke Welsh Corgi: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Liver lobe torsion (LLT) is a rare, potentially life-threatening condition in dogs and is reported most often in medium- to large-breed dogs. Neoplasia-associated LLT is unusual, and detailed descriptions of LLT associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are scarce. A 12-year-old spayed female Pembroke Welsh Corgi (9.5 kg) presented with acute collapse after several months of progressive lethargy and inappetence. Laboratory abnormalities included increased alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase activities and C-reactive protein concentration. Computed tomography (CT) identified a 7.2 × 6.7 × 6.5 cm mass arising from the left medial liver lobe, a whirl sign at the base of the mass and a non-enhancing hypoattenuating region consistent with necrosis. Midline celiotomy and left medial liver lobectomy were performed without detorsion. Cytology of abdominal effusion was consistent with a culture-negative inflammatory exudate. Histopathology confirmed HCC with extensive necrosis, and the examined surgical margin was free of neoplastic cells. The dog recovered uneventfully, was discharged on postoperative Day 4 and had no recurrence of clinical abnormalities at 1-year follow-up. This case highlights the apparent association between HCC and LLT and the unusual location of the torsion axis at the base of the mass rather than at the hepatic hilus, although causality cannot be established from a single case. CT visualisation of the whirl sign at this atypical site was instrumental in establishing the preoperative diagnosis and guiding surgical planning.

records.title: Bilateral Keratouveitis and Secondary Glaucoma in a Young Dog With Immune-Mediated Polyarthritis and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome.
records.abstract: A 7-month-old intact female mixed-breed dog presented emergently for inability to walk, lethargy, and vomiting. The patient was diagnosed with immune-mediated polyarthritis (IMPA) and secondary systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Bilateral keratouveitis and secondary glaucoma developed within 24 h of presentation. Thorough diagnostic testing failed to identify an underlying etiology. Despite aggressive medical management, the patient developed rapid vision loss. Due to poor visual prognosis and anticipated need for long-term medical management, both eyes were enucleated. Histopathological evaluation of both globes revealed severe corneal endothelial injury most consistent with endotheliitis with associated uveitis and endophthalmitis. Testing of ocular tissue with PCR and immunohistochemistry for canine adenovirus was negative, and comprehensive infectious disease screening, joint cultures, and ocular histopathology identified no other causative agents. Following enucleation, the dog systemically improved with anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial medical management. This report highlights a unique and severe case of bilateral keratouveitis with glaucoma following a systemic inflammatory event.

records.title: Anterior Segment OCT Diagnosis of Descemet's Membrane Detachment in a Cat With Suspected FIP-Associated Uveitis.
records.abstract: Persistent corneal edema in cats with anterior uveitis is often attributed to endothelial dysfunction; however, the underlying structural cause may not be apparent without advanced imaging. Descemet's membrane detachment (DMD) is rarely reported in cats and has not been well described in suspected feline infectious peritonitis (FIP)-associated uveitis. A 4-month-old intact male Norwegian Forest cat presented with severe unilateral granulomatous uveitis, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, diffuse stromal edema, and a 2+ aqueous flare. Aqueous humor PCR detected feline coronavirus RNA, although biotype testing did not confirm a mutation consistent with that associated with feline infectious peritonitis virus. As ocular inflammation progressed despite anti-inflammatory treatment, the nucleoside analog GS-441524 was administered along with anti-inflammatory and supportive ophthalmic treatment. Intraocular inflammation improved, but corneal edema persisted, prompting anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT), which revealed planar DMD. Serial AS-OCT monitored posterior corneal structural changes. Corneal edema gradually decreased, and Descemet's membrane reapposition was documented by AS-OCT approximately one year after the initial presentation. Corneal clarity and stability were maintained without clinically evident recurrence for 18 months after reapposition was confirmed. This case describes the AS-OCT diagnosis and serial documentation of DMD and subsequent Descemet's membrane reapposition in a cat with suspected FIP-associated uveitis. These findings highlight the value of AS-OCT for identifying and monitoring posterior corneal abnormalities, including DMD, in cats with severe anterior uveitis and persistent corneal edema. The relationships among suspected FIP-associated uveitis, treatment, and DMD could not be determined from this single case.

records.title: Meibomian Gland Epithelioma Mimicking Eyelid Squamous Cell Carcinoma in a Hereford-Cross Steer.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation and histopathology of a meibomian gland epithelioma that clinically resembled squamous cell carcinoma in a steer. A 15 year-old Hereford-Lowline cross steer presented for evaluation of an approximately 2 × 4 cm ulcerated, pedunculated eyelid mass arising from the right inferior eyelid margin. Excision of the mass followed by adjunctive cryotherapy was performed. The mass was submitted for histopathologic analysis. Histopathologic evaluation revealed the mass to be consistent with a meibomian gland epithelioma, a neoplastic proliferation of the basal/reserve cells of the meibomian gland. The steer recovered routinely from the procedure with no evidence of regrowth of the mass at 13 months post-operatively. Meibomian gland epitheliomas are one of the most common eyelid tumors of dogs; however, this is the first known report of a histologically confirmed meibomian gland epithelioma in cattle. Clinically, the mass resembled the appearance of squamous cell carcinoma, a common eyelid tumor in Hereford cattle. The clinical misclassification of a benign eyelid mass as squamous cell carcinoma could lead to unnecessary aggressive management such as enucleation, exenteration, or culling. This case confirms the importance of histopathologic analysis of excised tissues to reach an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment and follow-up plans.

records.title: Computed Tomographic Findings of Ischemic Necrosis of the Accessory Carpal Bone in a Dog.
records.journal: Veterinary radiology & ultrasound : the official journal of the American College of Veterinary Radiology and the International Veterinary Radiology Association
records.abstract: A 1-year-and-9-month-old Golden Retriever presented with a 9-month history of right thoracic limb lameness. Radiographs revealed a monostotic, expansile lesion of the right accessory carpal bone (ACB). A computed tomography (CT) confirmed the aggressive nature of the lesion, demonstrating multifocal moth-eaten osteolysis, sclerosis, periosteal reaction, and flexor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy. Differential diagnoses included the ischemic necrosis of the ACB, osteomyelitis, and primary bone neoplasia. Histopathology confirmed osteonecrosis. This case highlights the value of CT in evaluating aggressive carpal lesions and identifies ischemic necrosis as an important differential diagnosis. This case represents the first CT description of this disease in dogs.

records.title: Idiopathic Granulomatous Inflammation of the Periocular Structures in Four Dogs: Clinical, Histopathological, and Imaging Findings and Therapeutic Outcome.
records.abstract: To describe cases of canine idiopathic periocular granulomatous inflammation. Clinical records were reviewed. At the time of presentation, the four patients (German Shepherd dog, mixed breed, Magyar Vizsla, Hovawart) were 1.5-5 (mean 3.75) years old. All dogs were female; two were spayed. Lesions were unilateral in 3/4 cases. Dogs presented with ulcerated (1) or non-ulcerated (3) mass lesions affecting the periocular skin (3/4), medial canthal area (2/4), or third eyelid (1/4). Incisional biopsies revealed pyogranulomatous inflammation in three and granulomatous inflammation in one case. There was no evidence of microbial infection in the specimens. Patients received anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive dosages of systemic corticosteroids. Three dogs also received systemic cyclosporin (5 mg/kg, sid), and one dog received topical cyclosporin (0.1%, bid). One dog underwent surgical debulking of a circumscribed mass within the left lower eyelid prior to immunosuppressive therapy and developed an additional swelling on the left upper eyelid. Remission of clinical signs was achieved in all patients. Dogs were treated for 5 to 11 months (mean 8.7). No recurrence was reported in 4/4 patients during a mean follow-up period of 17.3 months. In 3/4patients, there was no recurrence within an average of 11 months after discontinuation of therapy. One dog was lost to follow-up. Idiopathic granulomatous inflammation is a differential diagnosis for periocular mass lesions. Its diagnosis is based on histopathology and the exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation.

records.title: Bilateral Third Eyelid Ectopic Cilia in a Maine Coon Cat.
records.abstract: To describe a case of a Maine Coon cat diagnosed with bilateral aberrant hairs consistent with ectopic cilia arising from the third eyelid. The history, clinical signs, examination findings, surgical procedures, and case outcome were reviewed. An eleven-month-old Maine Coon cat presented with a chronic history of bilateral epiphora and right blepharospasm. The left eye previously underwent upper and lower eyelid wedge excision to shorten the palpebral fissure and a partial Celsus-Hotz procedure to correct lower eyelid entropion. The right eye developed lower eyelid entropion shortly after and was surgically treated using the Read and Broun technique. Examination revealed a bilateral ocular discharge and follicular conjunctivitis; macroblepharon, permanent lower eyelid entropion associated with trichiasis, and non-ulcerative keratitis were present in the right eye. The upper and lower eyelid position was normal in the left eye. The right eye was treated with the Stades Diabolo technique and a partial Celsus-Hotz procedure. Inspection under general anesthesia revealed bilateral single aberrant hairs consistent with ectopic cilia on the palpebral surface of the third eyelid. A focal conjunctivectomy, including the ectopic cilium, was performed in each eye. Eyelid and conjunctival wounds healed uneventfully. Differential diagnoses for aberrant hair arising from the third eyelid conjunctiva include dermoid, choristoma, or ectopic cilium. Histology was declined due to financial constraints. Although not previously reported in the literature, given the clinical appearance, an ectopic cilium is the most likely diagnosis. Surgical excision was curative, with no recurrence of epiphora, conjunctivitis, or the entropion.

records.title: Corneal Sequestration and Bilateral Distichiasis in a Binturong (Arctictis binturong).
records.abstract: To report the first documented case of corneal sequestration and distichiasis in a binturong (Arctictis binturong), discuss implications of disease prevalence in a non-domestic feliform, and hypothesize on potential etiology and predisposing factors for corneal sequestration. A 15-year-old intact male binturong. Anesthetized physical examination and ophthalmic assessment were performed by board-certified specialists. Corneal cytology, culture and sensitivity, debridement of the sequestra in lieu of keratectomy, histopathology, and cryoepilation were performed, followed by 4 weeks of topical therapy. The patient was euthanized 3 years later for unrelated reasons, and a necropsy was performed. Examination found bilateral distichiasis. In the left cornea, two brown, ovoid lesions flanked an area of yellow infiltrate, all overlying a raised, ulcerated granulation bed. Corneal cytology identified neutrophils, cocci, and rare rods. Histopathology of the debrided tissue showed coagulative to lytic necrosis with intralesional gram-positive cocci, indicating sequestration and secondary infection. Aerobic culture yielded Staphylococcus delphini and Streptococcus acidominimus. Photo updates 4 weeks post-operation showed resolution of clinical signs. Later, necropsy and histology showed chronic ocular changes without recurrence of sequestra. Clinical and histopathologic findings identified corneal sequestration, with chronic irritation secondary to distichiasis as a suspected factor. Surgical debridement and cryoepilation achieved long-term clinical resolution, with only mild distichiae regrowth and no sequestration recurrence after 3 years. Corneal sequestration is thought to predominantly affect domestic cats (Felis catus); this report expands the clinical relevance of corneal sequestration to an exotic species and supports chronic corneal irritation as a predisposing factor.

records.title: Removal of a Posteriorly Luxated Lens Using Pars Plana Vitrectomy and Perfluorocarbon Liquid: A Case Report.
records.abstract: To report a case of canine posterior lens luxation in which the intact lens was successfully floated using perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) combined with pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and subsequently removed. A client-owned 7-year-old castrated female Italian Greyhound presented with rapidly progressive bilateral posterior lens luxation. In the right eye, via a three-port 25-gauge pars plana approach, the vitreous was removed and PFCL was injected beneath the luxated lens to float the intact lens from the retinal surface to the pupillary plane. The lens was subsequently removed by intracapsular lens extraction through a limbal incision using a cryoprobe. At the final 6-month follow-up examination, vision was preserved, and no retinal detachment or other significant postoperative complications were observed. In this case, combining PPV and PFCL was an effective technique for managing posterior lens luxation and enabled successful removal of the intact luxated lens.

records.title: Corneal stromal metastasis of urothelial carcinoma in a dog.
records.abstract: A 15-year-old intact male Miniature Dachshund presented with severe hematuria. Clinical evaluations of this dog raised the suspicion of a malignant bladder tumor, and corneal stromal opacity was observed in the left eye. Because of the critical condition, the dog died on the day of presentation, after which a necropsy was performed. Necropsy and histopathological examinations confirmed urothelial carcinoma (UC) in the bladder. Moreover, the corneal stromal opacity represented a metastatic lesion of UC, and similar metastatic lesions were identified at 13 other sites. The UC in this dog was considered clinically highly malignant based on its rapid clinical course and the presence of multiple metastatic sites. This highly malignant nature may have contributed to the corneal stromal metastasis. This is an extremely rare case of corneal stromal metastasis from canine UC.

records.title: Feline cutaneous mast cell tumor with extensive macrophage-associated cell-in-cell structures.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: An 8-y-old, castrated male Korean Shorthair cat was presented to a veterinary clinic for evaluation of a cutaneous mass on the left inner thigh. Microscopic examination revealed a poorly circumscribed dermal neoplasm composed of poorly granulated, pleomorphic neoplastic mast cells with frequent cell-in-cell structures. Notably, viable neoplastic mast cells were engulfed by large macrophages, indicating a specific form of the cell-in-cell phenomenon. Immunohistochemistry for c-KIT, IBA1, and cleaved caspase-3 was used to support the diagnosis. To our knowledge, cell-in-cell phenomenon has not been previously described in feline cutaneous mast cell tumors, nor has the clinical outcome of such cases been reported.

records.title: Diagnosis of feline platynosomosis: case series and literature review.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: Platynosomosis is a parasitic disease of cats and other animal species, caused by trematodes of the genus  Platynosomum . These flukes can infect the liver parenchyma, biliary ducts, and gallbladder. In cats, this parasite is most commonly associated with inapparent infections; however, clinical infections with cholangiohepatitis have also been described.  Platynosomum  spp. are also related to the development of cholangiocarcinoma. Here, we describe 6 cases of cats parasitized by  Platynosomum illiciens . Four of these cats were also infected with feline leukemia virus; 5 were parasitized with  Spirometra mansoni , 4 with  Ancylostoma  sp., and 1 with  Dirofilaria immitis.  Clinical and coprologic evaluations were performed on all individuals. Five cats had severe clinical decline, which prompted euthanasia. On autopsy, these 5 animals had diffuse cholangiohepatitis with intralesional trematodes. Gross and microscopic lesions, parasite and egg morphology, PCR, and DNA sequencing with a Bayesian inference phylogenetic tree and haplotype network confirmed a diagnosis of platynosomosis caused by  P. illiciens .

records.title: Clostridium perfringens  gas gangrene in a canine splenic liposarcoma.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: Histotoxic clostridial infections occur when clostridial spores germinate in anaerobic tissue environments and release a variety of extracellular toxins, causing necrosis, secondary inflammation, and often death. These infections are seen in humans and animals, especially ruminants and horses, but are rare in dogs. An 11-y-old, intact male Border Collie-cross dog was inappetent and lethargic after abdominal blunt-force trauma. Clinical examination and imaging revealed a splenic mass containing gas and an abdominal effusion, identified cytologically as a neutrophilic exudate. At splenectomy, an area on the anti-hilar surface of the mass was abscessed, with inspissated material on the mass surface and in the omentum. Histopathology identified a splenic liposarcoma with areas of necrosis, suppuration, emphysema, and colonization by large gram-positive bacilli. These were identified as  Clostridium perfringens  by immunohistochemistry. The bacteria are presumed to have translocated from the bowel and germinated in a region of tumor necrosis secondary to traumatic ischemia. To our knowledge, gas gangrene has not been reported previously within a visceral tumor in a dog.

records.title: Oxidative stress and immunomarkers in equine dermal melanomatosis: single-case comparison with healthy individual.
records.abstract: Dermal melanomatosis is a common tumor in grey horses, characterized by cutaneous/subcutaneous lesions with metastatic potential. While clinically well-described, oxidative stress involvement remains poorly understood. This case report compared oxidative stress markers and antioxidant enzymes' activities in total protein extracts from melanomatosis lesions (grey horse) versus healthy control skin (black horse), alongside histopathology and immunohistochemistry, to correlate oxidative imbalance and tumor behavior. Melanomatosis tissue exhibited decreased antioxidant defenses confirmed by catalase (CAT) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) reduced activities, with 29% lower glutathione (GSH) levels. Oxidative damage markers increased in melanomatosis tissue: malondialdehyde (MDA) rising by 73% and advanced oxidation protein products (AOPP) by 56%. Histology confirmed melanocytic proliferation, supported by moderate positive S100 (highly sensitive melanocytic marker) and low proliferation rate (8% positive to proliferation marker Ki-67). These findings suggest oxidative stress was involved in melanomatosis pathophysiology in this case, highlighting the potential relevance of these markers for further investigation.

records.title: Characterization of  Escherichia marmotae , a novel pathogen causing urinary tract infection in a dog.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: Escherichia  is one of the most studied bacterial genera and includes several clinically significant pathogenic species. Unique strategies have evolved in members of this genus to allow their survival within different niches. Although initially the  Escherichia  cryptic clades (CCs) I-VIII were identified as environmental bacteria, they have been found as commensals and opportunistic pathogens in animals and humans. Notably, members of the  Escherichia  CCs are commonly mistaken for  E. coli  when using standard microbiologic techniques for species identification. We used whole-genome sequencing to correctly identify  E. marmotae -a member of the  Escherichia  CCs-that was initially misidentified as  E. coli  as the causative agent of a urinary tract infection (UTI) in a female dog. The isolate had phenotypic and genotypic resistance to cefalexin-an antibiotic used commonly for the treatment of uncomplicated UTIs-and carried a set of virulence factors also present in uropathogenic  E. coli , which would explain the capacity of the organism to colonize the urinary tract. As a relatively new species that is phenotypically very similar to  E. coli , it is quite possible that  E. marmotae  infections may be underreported or misidentified. We hope that our work alerts veterinarians to consider  E. marmotae  as a possible cause of UTIs in dogs, especially because this could affect treatment decisions. Additionally, our findings broaden the current understanding of the  E. marmotae  ecology and host range.

records.title: Disseminated histiocytic sarcoma in 2 FeLV-positive cats in Brazil.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: Histiocytic sarcomas (HSs) are uncommon malignant neoplasms in cats, typically affecting older animals and not previously associated with feline leukemia virus (FeLV). Here, we describe 2 cases of disseminated HS in young FeLV-positive domestic shorthair cats that clinically and grossly mimicked lymphoma. Case 1, a 1-y-old female cat, was presented with hemiplegia and dysuria and was euthanized because of the clinical suspicion of spinal lymphoma. Case 2, a 4-y-old male cat, had hyporexia, ocular abnormalities, and bilateral renal enlargement and was euthanized because of the clinical suspicion of renal and ocular lymphoma. Both cases tested positive for feline leukemia virus (FeLV) infection with a SNAP test. At autopsy, case 1 had a white, irregular, intradural spinal cord mass at the C6-C7 segment, and case 2 had coalescing, unencapsulated, white nodules that effaced both renal cortices, along with uveal thickening in the left eye with hyphema. Both cases had highly pleomorphic neoplastic round-cell proliferation in neoplastic masses, with strong cytoplasmic labeling for vimentin and IBA1 on immunohistochemistry and no CD20 or CD3 labeling, confirming disseminated HS. The neoplastic cells also had strong cytoplasmic immunolabeling for FeLV, suggesting a possible oncogenic role of FeLV in feline HSs.

records.title: A Rare Case of a Concurrent Mandibular Odontogenic Keratocyst and Oral Rhabdomyosarcoma in a Young Cat.
records.abstract: A 3-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat was presented with acute pain during feeding and with hypersalivation, without any history of trauma. Histopathological evaluation identified features consistent with an odontogenic keratocyst and concurrently confirmed the presence of a rhabdomyosarcoma. records.title: From inference to proof: nanopore sequencing confirms zoonotic Neisseria Zoodegmatis peritonitis after cat bite-related contamination in a patient on automated peritoneal dialysis.
records.abstract: Peritoneal dialysis (PD)-associated peritonitis caused by zoonotic pathogens is uncommon and diagnostically challenging. Neisseria zoodegmatis, a Gram-negative coccobacillus residing in the oral flora of cats and dogs, has been reported only once previously in PD-associated peritonitis, with zoonotic transmission inferred but unproven. We report the case of a 90-year-old patient receiving automated PD who developed peritonitis following cat bite-related transfer-set damage, with partial response to empirical therapy and subsequent relapse. Conventional culture and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry identified N. zoodegmatis, confirmed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing from colony isolates and PD effluent. Intermediate β-lactam susceptibility prompted escalation to carbapenem-based therapy. Third-generation nanopore sequencing demonstrated N. zoodegmatis as the dominant organism in PD effluent and identified the identical species in feline saliva, establishing molecular concordance. Sustained remission required strict environmental control. This is the second reported case of Neisseria zoodegmatis PD-associated peritonitis and the first one with molecular proof of zoonotic transmission, highlighting the selective role of long-read sequencing in complex or relapsing peritonitis, the need for antimicrobial reassessment after suspicion of pet-related contamination, and the importance of environmental intervention in preventing recurrence.

records.title: First molecular characterization of Echinococcus granulosus sensu stricto genotype G1 from a common chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) in the Kuwait Zoo.

records.title: Radiation therapy for persistent or progressive mediastinal lymphoma after chemotherapy in FeLV-positive cats: a retrospective case series of four cats.
records.abstract: Mediastinal lymphoma in feline leukaemia virus (FeLV)-positive cats is associated with a poor prognosis, and therapeutic options may be limited when adequate disease control is not achieved with chemotherapy. The efficacy of radiation therapy in this setting has not been established. Medical records were retrospectively reviewed for FeLV-positive cats diagnosed with mediastinal lymphoma between November 2018 and December 2024 that had persistent or progressive mediastinal disease after chemotherapy and were subsequently treated with radiation therapy. Treatment response was assessed by computed tomography using the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST). Three of four cats (75%) responded to radiation therapy (two complete responses, one partial response). Respiratory signs improved rapidly in three cats (median 5 days). Local disease control was achieved in most cases; however, three cats developed progression at other sites. Survival times were 45, 150 and 352 days in cats that died, and one cat remained alive for >626 days at the time of last follow-up. No severe radiation-related adverse effects were documented during the available follow-up, although systematic evaluation of late radiation toxicity was not possible. Radiation therapy may provide local control and rapid palliation of respiratory signs in FeLV-positive cats with persistent or progressive mediastinal lymphoma after chemotherapy. Further studies with larger cohorts are warranted.

records.title: Mapping the preclinical therapeutic landscape of cirrhotic portal hypertension: a systematic evidence map.
records.abstract: Portal hypertension has a limited pharmacological armamentarium despite decades of preclinical therapeutic research. We mapped the experimental architecture of this literature, independently of reported treatment efficacy. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched from inception to March 31, 2026. Two independent title-and-abstract screening procedures identified 833 records retained by at least one screen; 540 formed a concordant core retained by both. Records were classified using a prespecified taxonomy of therapeutic strategy, intervention modality, animal model, species, sex, treatment schedule and reporting features. Global counts included all records; variable-specific distributions used available-case denominators. Treatment effects were not extracted. Among records with classifiable mechanisms (n=709), vasoactive/neurohumoral (29.1%), NO-cGMP/endothelial (23.8%) and antifibrotic/HSC-extracellular-matrix strategies (20.0%) represented 72.9%. Among records reporting the relevant variable, rats accounted for 82.7% (677/819), males only for 85.9% (548/638), and CCl 4 , bile-duct ligation/cholestatic models and thioacetamide for 45.2%, 30.3% and 10.6% (n=568), respectively. Randomization and blinding were identifiable in indexed information for 5.3% and 0.1% of all records. Principal distributions were preserved in the concordant core. Preclinical portal-hypertension research has generated mechanistic diversity on a narrow experimental foundation. Broader use of both sexes, etiologically diverse models, repeated dosing, rigorous design and complementary human-based platforms may strengthen translation.

records.title: Wound myiasis caused by Lucilia spp. (Diptera: Calliphoridae) in a dog and a cat in Korea.
records.abstract: This study presents 2 cases of wound myiasis in a dog and a cat involving morphological and molecular identification in Korea. A 7-year-old male Jindo mix dog, Canis familiaris, was admitted to a veterinary clinic in Yangsan-si, Gyeongsangnam-do, Korea, in July 2024. records.title: Case series: Superficial lipomatous hamartoma in dogs and cats is a previously unreported NLCS-like dermal lesion.
records.abstract: In humans nevus lipomatosus cutaneous superficialis (NLCS) is a rare, benign dermal hamartoma characterized by aggregates of adipose tissue within the dermis without any connection to the subcutaneous tissue. Over the course of one and a half years, six cases (five in dogs, one in a cat), resembling NLCS-like lesions, were examined. In this report, we compare these cases to the human condition regarding macroscopic features, histopathology, sex, and age of the affected patients. In all cases, the dermal lesions were composed of aggregates of well-differentiated adipocytes within the dermis. Given the morphological similarity to the lesion in humans, the term "nevus lipomatosus superficialis-like lesion" might be appropriate. However, given the controversial use of the term 'nevus' in veterinary medicine and a potential for confusion with pigmented lesion, we propose the term "superficial lipomatous hamartoma" for this entity.

records.title: Case Report: Concurrent ventricular septal defect, pulmonic stenosis, and intrapulmonary arteriovenous anastomoses in a Korean raccoon dog ( Nyctereutes procyonoides koreensis ).
records.abstract: A 3-month-old intact male Korean raccoon dog ( Nyctereutes procyonoides koreensis ) was rescued and admitted to the Jeonbuk Wildlife Rescue Center with lethargy, dehydration, and dermatologic lesions consistent with  Sarcoptes scabiei  infestation. Physical examination detected a grade IV/VI systolic murmur, and thoracic radiography revealed generalized cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography identified a perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with left-to-right shunting. Although no distinct structural abnormalities of the pulmonic valve were observed, increased pulmonic flow velocity (3.87 m/s), mild pulmonic regurgitation (1.68 m/s), and post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery supported a diagnosis of pulmonic stenosis (PS). Agitated saline contrast echocardiography demonstrated intrapulmonary arteriovenous anastomoses (IPAVAs), with microbubbles appearing in the left heart after the fourth cardiac cycle; this shunting decreased following oxygen supplementation. Five weeks later, thoracic radiography demonstrated a reduction in cardiac silhouette size, although cardiomegaly persisted. Echocardiography demonstrated progression of the VSD to bidirectional shunting. Systolic doming of the pulmonic valve, together with increased pulmonic flow velocity (4.39 m/s) and pulmonic regurgitation velocity (2.07 m/s), indicated worsening PS. Repeat agitated saline contrast echocardiography revealed microbubbles in the left heart within four cardiac cycles and in the abdominal aorta, indicating a right-to-left shunt component consistent with bidirectional shunting. These findings were attenuated after oxygen supplementation. The Korean raccoon dog subsequently died during anesthetic induction for further diagnostic imaging. Postmortem examination confirmed a perimembranous VSD and type A valvular PS characterized by fused commissures, with concurrent right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, and interventricular septal thickening. To our knowledge, this case report is the first to describe the concurrence of VSD, PS, and IPAVAs in a Korean raccoon dog. It suggests that progressive PS may contribute to reversal of shunting across a VSD.

records.title: Candida albicans  Urinary Tract Infection with Suspected Fungal Hepatobiliary Disease in an Immunosuppressed Dog: A Case Report.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: Fungal urinary tract infections (UTIs) are uncommon in dogs and are typically associated with immunocompromised patients or those with other predisposing factors. Fungal hepatobiliary disease is rarely reported in the veterinary literature. This case report describes a dog on dual immunosuppressive therapy for suspected immune-mediated polyarthritis that developed a hepatopathy suspected to represent bacterial hepatobiliary disease and was subsequently treated with prolonged amoxicillin-clavulanate therapy. Following treatment, the dog developed marked hepatocellular enzyme elevations together with a  Candida albicans  UTI. Given the patient's progressive hepatocellular injury, clinical signs, history of immunosuppression and antibiotic therapy, concurrent fungal hepatobiliary involvement was suspected. Following initiation of oral fluconazole, the fungal UTI resolved, and there was marked improvement, with subsequent normalisation of ALT and ALP activities. Although the temporal association between antifungal treatment and clinical and biochemical improvement raised suspicion of concurrent fungal hepatobiliary involvement, simultaneous discontinuation of amoxicillin-clavulanate, substantial reduction in prednisolone dose, and continuation of hepatoprotective therapy precluded attribution of the improvement specifically to antifungal treatment. This case highlights the potential for opportunistic fungal disease in immunosuppressed dogs, particularly following prolonged antimicrobial exposure, and illustrates the diagnostic challenges associated with suspected hepatobiliary involvement.

records.title: Case Report: Long term multimodality treatment of canine hepatocellular carcinoma with serial monitoring of serum alpha-fetoprotein.
records.abstract: A 13-year-old spayed female Shih Tzu presented with a several-month history of progressively increasing liver enzyme activities concurrent with managed hyperadrenocorticism. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) was confirmed via histopathological examination of an ultrasound-guided tru-cut biopsy, accompanied by a markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) concentration. Molecular targeted therapy with olaparib was initiated since complete surgical resection was unachievable due to tumor adherence to the caudal vena cava and conventional chemotherapy has limited efficacy for canine HCC, based on genomic profiling. Postoperatively, olaparib and canine interleukin-15 (cIL-15) immunotherapy were instituted to control potential micrometastases. The patient achieved clinical and radiographic stability for a 10-month follow-up period, accompanied by a significant drop in serum AFP levels. However, following the discontinuation of cIL-15 and subsequent reduction of olaparib dosage because of suspected adverse effects, serum AFP levels rebounded progressively, and tumor recurrence was confirmed via ultrasonography. The patient died 20 months after the initial detection of the mass. This case describes the clinical course of canine HCC managed with a multimodal therapeutic approach and highlights the potential utility of serum AFP as an adjunctive biomarker for disease monitoring.

records.title: Mammary secretory carcinoma in a female domestic rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus): histopathological and immunohistochemical features.
records.abstract: Secretory carcinoma of the breast is a rare histological subtype in women and is uncommon in female dogs and cats, with only two cases described in female dogs and one case described in a cat. Microscopic evaluation revealed a non-encapsulated, well-demarcated neoplastic proliferation composed of epithelial cells arranged in solid and tubular patterns, supported by a delicate fibrous connective tissue stroma. The neoplastic cells had slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, frequently containing large, well-demarcated vacuoles that displaced the nucleus to the periphery, giving the cells a signet-ring-like appearance. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) histochemical staining, performed with and without diastase digestion, showed positivity in the intracellular and extracellular secretory material in both approaches. Immunohistochemical evaluation was performed for the markers α-lactalbumin, Ki-67, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and COX-2. Positive cytoplasmic immunolabeling for α-lactalbumin was observed in neoplastic cells and in intracellular and extracellular secretory material, confirming their secretory nature. The diagnosis of secretory carcinoma was established based on the association of histopathological, histochemical, and immunohistochemical features. Considering the secretory features of the mammary gland in rabbits, secretory carcinoma should be included in the differential diagnosis of mammary carcinomas with prominent secretory activity in this species.

records.title: Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasonography of Orbital and Intraocular Pathologies in 24 Dogs and 6 Cats.
records.abstract: Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (CEUS) is a noninvasive and relatively safe imaging technique to assess ocular perfusion, showing high sensitivity and specificity for tumor characterization in human oncology, while reports on its application in canine and feline diseased eyes are limited. This study aimed to describe the CEUS features of orbital and intraocular pathologies in dogs and cats in order to evaluate its diagnostic value in detecting and characterizing various lesions. CEUS examinations of 30 animals (24 dogs, 6 cats) were evaluated retrospectively. Following B-mode ultrasonography, CEUS examinations utilizing sulfur hexafluoride were performed. Pathologies were categorized in one of the following groups: orbital neoplastic lesions, orbital inflammatory lesions, intraocular neoplastic lesions, intraocular inflammatory lesions and retinal detachment. Qualitative perfusion parameters, contrast intensity, enhancement pattern, perfusion type and time to wash-in and wash-out were evaluated. CEUS detected vascularization in orbital and intraocular pathologies, with variable enhancement characteristics. Persistent vascularization was observed in all cases of retinal detachment. In orbital and intraocular neoplastic lesions, CEUS improved lesion localization, assessment of interactions with surrounding tissues and tissue perfusion. records.title: Anatomopathological features of uterine tube adenoma in a female dog.

records.title: Sequential thoracoscopic thoracic duct occlusion and intra-abdominal lymphatic intervention for feline refractory idiopathic chylothorax.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Surgical management of feline idiopathic chylothorax remains unpredictable, with reported success rates varying widely despite combined procedures. A 2nd surgery was conducted to achieve definitive thoracic duct ligation using sutures combined with additional clipping, yet the effusion remained refractory. This comprehensive, minimally invasive approach, enhanced by real-time ICG visualization, offers a potent therapeutic option when conventional, single-cavity treatments fail. records.title: A rare case of aphakia associated with anterior segment malformation in a cocker spaniel puppy.

records.title: Canine Maxillofacial Parosteal Osteosarcoma: A Retrospective Case Evaluation in 10 Dogs.
records.abstract: Parosteal osteosarcoma (OSA) is a subtype of surface OSA that is considered slow growing with a less aggressive biological behavior compared to central OSA and, therefore, carries a better prognosis with surgical excision. Parosteal OSA has a predilection for the skull in dogs with documented more frequent occurrences on the zygoma, maxilla, or coronoid process of the mandible, all of which present unique challenges to the oral surgeon. Ten cases of parosteal OSA of the canine maxillofacial bones are summarized and discussed in this report. The most common bone of origin was the caudal maxilla and/or zygoma in 50% of tumors. Exophthalmos was a prominent clinical sign noted in 40% of dogs. Median survival time was 14 months, with a one-year survival rate of 60%. Metastasis to the lungs was suspected in three cases. The histopathological diagnosis of parosteal OSA is crucially dependent on diagnostic imaging. When a primary bone tumor of the maxillofacial bones is suspected, it is essential for the oral surgeon and pathologist to collaborate to provide informed guidance on surgical planning, anticipated long-term outcomes, and clinical monitoring for these patients. The goals of this retrospective study are to identify key clinical and radiographic features, improve recognition for accurate diagnosis, and establish treatment recommendations for canine maxillofacial parosteal OSA.

records.title: Adjunctive Huperzine A for owner-directed aggression associated with hypersensitivity-hyperactivity syndrome in a dog: a case report.
records.abstract: A 7-month-old female Golden Retriever was referred for owner-directed aggression occurring during intense emotional arousal and characterised by a limited ability to down-regulate arousal and inhibit impulsive motor patterns. Clinical assessment was consistent with hypersensitivity-hyperactivity syndrome (HSHA), an ADHD-like neurodevelopmental condition described in dogs and associated with hyperactivity, impulsivity and reduced behavioural inhibition. A multimodal treatment plan including environmental management and structured behaviour modification was implemented. Fluoxetine was initiated at approximately 0.9 mg/kg/day and was associated with a marked reduction in aggressive incidents and improved arousal regulation. A subsequent attempt to increase the fluoxetine dose to improve residual impulsivity resulted in a 50% reduction of appetite (approximately), necessitating a return to the prior dose. Huperzine A, a Chinese club moss alkaloid and centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with additional neuroprotective effects, was then added at 200 μg orally every 12 h. Following adjunctive huperzine A, the dog showed further improvement in behavioural inhibition and impulse control with additional reductions in arousal-linked impulsive behaviour and aggression and no reported adverse effects. This case highlights HSHA-associated owner-directed aggression and suggests that adjunctive huperzine A may be a useful option when dose-limiting adverse effects prevent optimisation of SSRI therapy.

records.title: [Pasteurella multocida septic arthritis in a native joint: Management dilemmas in a penicillin-allergic patient].
records.abstract: Pasteurella multocida is a common zoonotic, but it can also lead to invasive forms such as septic arthritis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. records.title: Clinical manifestations and management of Androctonus bicolor envenomation in a dog: A previously undescribed clinical case.

records.abstract: The black fat tailed scorpion (Androctonus bicolor) is one of the most venomous native scorpion species in Israel. Three days post admission the dog presented marked clinical improvement and was discharged, however, five days after discharge, the dog was re-presented with tremors, inappetence, hematochezia, hyperthermia, mild tachycardia with occasional ventricular premature complexes, and labored breathing. Bloodwork revealed an elevated C-reactive protein concentration and mild increased pancreatic lipase activity, consistent with systemic inflammation and mild pancreatitis. Supportive therapy was instituted, and clinical improvement was observed within 24 hours from the second admission. The dog was discharged and remained well. records.title: Pleural effusion associated with Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection in a splenectomised dog.
records.abstract: Strongyloides stercoralis is a soil-transmitted helminth that is increasingly reported in dogs across Europe. While most infections are subclinical, hyperinfection syndrome, marked by excessive larval proliferation and systemic spread, can occur in immunocompromised hosts. The HVR-IV haplotype A is found in both dogs and humans, characterizing the zoonotic population of S. stercoralis. Respiratory signs worsened despite combined fenbendazole and escalating ivermectin treatment, requiring euthanasia. Post-mortem examination revealed chronic granulomatous pneumonia, a pulmonary carcinomatous nodule, lymphoplasmacytic enterocolitis, and glomerulonephritis. It highlights the importance of including strongyloidiasis in differential diagnoses of dogs with respiratory and gastrointestinal signs, particularly in animals with compromised immunity or relevant travel history.

records.title: The benefits of multidisciplinary collaboration in the successful management of two complex feline cases.
records.abstract: Despite a frequent misconception that behavioural concerns are diagnoses of exclusion, medical conditions and behavioural disorders are frequently inter-related. In human medicine, the 'multidisciplinary team' approach (MDTA) is considered the most efficacious way of managing patients with complex and chronic health conditions. Detailed diagnostics explored dermatological, behavioural and neurological differential diagnoses. No single diagnosis could completely explain the feline patient's clinical signs or behaviour. A treatment plan involving medication, environmental management and behaviour modification was implemented to improve her health and welfare. Feline patient 2, a 3-year-old spayed domestic long-haired cat, presented after surgical removal of a trichobezoar (second surgery). The diagnostic work-up considered dermatological, behavioural and gastrointestinal causes. A working diagnosis was made of anxiety disorder with possible compounding factors of gastrointestinal and dermatological conditions. The treatment plan included medication, environmental management and behaviour modification. The overgrooming and fur ingestion behaviours resolved, and long-term strategies maintained physical and emotional health and welfare. Without the MDTA, neither feline patient would have received effective care. Using the MDTA for managing complex veterinary cases provides skilful assessment in determining aetiologies, treatment of complex conditions, and identification and management of contributing factors, which may affect and predict flare-ups. records.title: Variations on the rostral labial pivot flap for reconstruction of maxillary lip defects in four dogs.
records.abstract: To describe the technique and outcome of a rostral labial pivot flap variant in dogs. Four dogs with rostral lip/paranasal defect underwent rostral labial pivot flap. Short case series. Rostral lip and paranasal defects with concurrent nasal mucosal involvement resulting from tumor resection were reconstructed using the rostral labial pivot flap and its variants, including incorporation of a mucosal island flap ± nasal rotation flap for modification of lip heights. Medical records were reviewed for all dogs that underwent tumor resection followed by reconstruction with a rostral labial pivot flap technique and its modifications. The rostral labial pivot flap and its variants provided acceptable outcomes in four dogs for reconstruction of rostral lip and paranasal defects. Incorporation of a mucosal island flap was effective for nasal mucosal reconstruction, and use of a nasal rotation flap to reduce tension and address lip height discrepancy resulted in acceptable outcomes. Two dogs experienced minor complications, including an oronasal fistula and mild narial stenosis, neither of which was associated with clinical signs. All dogs were considered to have normal function and quality of life at follow-up. The rostral labial pivot flap can be a reasonable and adaptable option for reconstruction of rostral lip and paranasal defects in dogs. Acceptable cosmetic and functional outcomes with low morbidity were observed in this series; however, additional cases are needed to better define success rates and complications.

records.title: Successful management of nesidioblastosis in a dog with persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia following staged bilateral partial pancreatectomies.
records.abstract: Nesidioblastosis is a rare but important differential diagnosis for hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia in dogs, a condition most commonly associated with insulinoma. A nine-year-old spayed female dog was presented with recurrent episodes of collapse and documented hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Diagnostic imaging failed to identify a pancreatic mass, prompting exploratory laparotomy with left partial pancreatectomy and regional lymphadenectomy. Histopathological examination excluded insulinoma and established a diagnosis of nesidioblastosis. Although clinical signs initially resolved following surgery, hypoglycemia recurred 45 days later, prompting a right partial pancreatectomy. Following the second procedure, the patient remained euglycemic and free of clinical signs, without evidence of clinical diabetes mellitus or exocrine pancreatic insufficiency throughout an eight-month follow-up period. This case underscores the importance of considering nesidioblastosis in dogs with hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia when a pancreatic mass is not identified. Furthermore, this case suggests that recurrence after unilateral partial pancreatectomy may occur because of the diffuse nature of nesidioblastosis. In this patient, staged bilateral partial pancreatectomy was associated with sustained glycemic control and clinical remission, without clinically apparent endocrine or exocrine pancreatic dysfunction during an eight-month follow-up period.

records.title: Surgical management of an unstable occipital condyle fracture in a dog using a patient-specific CNC-milled titanium implant: a case report.
records.abstract: A 10-year-old castrated male Pomeranian was evaluated after a fall and presented with tetraparesis, dysphagia, and headturn. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a right occipital condyle fracture that caused brainstem compression and cerebellar infarction from a displaced bony fragment. According to the Anderson and Montesano classification in human medicine, this case was presumed to be Type 3, indicating instability, and surgical correction was considered. A bone fragment located in the medulla oblongata was left  in situ  owing to the potential risk of severe complications from removal. Occipitocervical stabilization surgery was performed to prevent further damage from instability. A patient-specific titanium implant was designed by CAD and fabricated by CNC milling, and screws were applied to the occiput and C1 vertebra using standard techniques, whereas a screw was inserted transversely into the C2 spinous process to minimize the risk of implant failure from neck flexion. Postoperative computed tomography (CT) confirmed proper implant placement without neural injury. Over time, the patient showed improvements in hypoglossal dysfunction and gait, and was discharged on postoperative day five. Occipital condyle fractures are rare in both veterinary and human medicine, with most cases classified as type 1 or 2, and typically do not require surgical intervention. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed description of surgical stabilization of an occipital condyle fracture in a dog using a patient-specific, CNC-milled titanium implant. Conservative management of occipital condyle fracture and surgical stabilization of craniocervical junction fractures have been described previously, and the contribution of the present report lies in the implant design and fabrication workflow rather than in the surgical management of craniocervical injury  per se .

records.title: Total ear canal ablation for the treatment of auricular hemangiosarcoma in a cat: case report.
records.abstract: Ear neoplasms are growths that commonly affect light-coated, unpigmented felines exposed to prolonged sunlight. Another factor associated with these growths is the constant tissue trauma caused by intense pruritus in cases of chronic otitis. Any tissue making up the structure of the pinna can undergo changes and initiate pathogenic cell proliferation. In this context, cutaneous hemangiosarcomas may arise from alterations in the ear's vascular endothelium, albeit less frequently. This report describes the case of a 12-year-old, white, mixed-breed cat with a history of prior pinnectomy and local recurrence. To treat the new lesion, total ear canal ablation combined with cryotherapy of the surgical bed was selected to maximize recurrence-free survival. Histopathological analysis of the surgical specimen confirmed a moderate grade hemangiosarcoma associated with chronic otitis, with clear margins. The patient was referred to for oncological follow-up and remains free of recurrence one year after the procedure.

records.title: Staged caval occlusion enabling en bloc right divisional hepatectomy in two dogs with hepatocellular carcinoma.
records.abstract: To describe staged pre-renal caudal vena cava (CVC) occlusion before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental caval resection in two dogs with right divisional hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) involving the CVC. Two client-owned, 11-year-old neutered male dogs (Siberian Husky and Shih Tzu). Short case series. Dog 1 (Siberian Husky) had prior hemoperitoneum and biopsy-confirmed HCC; dog 2 (Shih Tzu) had persistent liver enzyme elevations and a suspected hepatic tumor. Computed tomography (CT) showed right divisional masses (91.8 × 122.3 × 101.4 mm; 77.0 × 94.8 × 70.2 mm) with CVC compression or involvement and no pre-existing collateral venous return. A percutaneously controlled hydraulic occluder was placed around the pre-renal CVC. Gradual outpatient occlusion was performed over 79 and 44 days while monitoring saphenous venous pressure, renal values, and hindlimb edema. Complete CVC occlusion and collateralization were confirmed by CT before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental CVC resection. Macroscopically complete resection was achieved in both dogs. Complete HCC resection was confirmed histopathologically. Morbidity was limited to transient wound exudation in dog 1 and transient ascites in dog 2. No recurrence or metastasis was identified in dog 1 during follow-up. In dog 2, no clinical signs suggestive of recurrence or metastasis were reported. Survival after hepatectomy was 352 and 2467 days. Staged pre-renal CVC occlusion may establish collateral venous return and permit planned en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental CVC resection in carefully selected dogs with right divisional HCC involving the CVC.

records.title: Urothelial Carcinoma in a Cat with Bilateral Ectopic Ureters.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: A 10-year-old neutered female Maine Coon was presented with haematuria, weight loss, polyuria/polydipsia and progressive azotaemia. Diagnostic imaging revealed bilateral renal pelvic dilation, ureteral distension and ectopic ureters. Bacterial pyelonephritis was diagnosed, but the azotaemia progressed despite antibiotic therapy, and suspected ureteral obstruction prompted surgical ureteral reimplantation. The visualisation of omental nodules and thickening of the ectopic right ureterovesicular junction intraoperatively raised suspicion of malignancy, and histopathology revealed urothelial carcinoma with carcinomatosis. Clinicians should consider malignancy as a differential in cats with ectopic ureters and an atypical or refractory clinical course.

records.abstract: Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial origin that is infrequently reported in cats, accounting for less than 2% of nonhematopoietic neoplasms. While HSA is the tumor most commonly reported to metastasize to the brain in dogs, intracranial involvement in cats remains rare, with only one previously documented metastatic case. records.title: Cytologic and Cytochemical Characterization of Blue-Green Neutrophilic Inclusions in a Dog with Suspected Transfusion-Associated Hemolysis.
records.abstract: An 11-year-old castrated male Maltese dog presented with acute lethargy and non-regenerative anemia. Despite immunosuppressive therapy and an initial packed red blood cell (pRBC) transfusion, hematocrit levels progressively declined after transient improvement. A second transfusion was administered following compatible crossmatch testing. Within 24 h of the second transfusion, a transfusion-associated hemolytic episode was suspected due to a rapid hematocrit decline, pigmenturia, hyperbilirubinemia, and autoagglutination. Peripheral blood smear revealed neutrophils containing coarse blue-green cytoplasmic inclusions. Special staining and autofluorescence microscopy supported lipid-rich, acid-fast, and autofluorescent properties of the inclusions. Prussian blue staining showed iron-positive granular material in the hemolytic sample, but the intraneutrophilic inclusions did not show distinct Prussian blue reactivity, making hemosiderin-rich sideroleukocytes unlikely to fully explain the findings. Similar inclusions have recently been characterized in dogs, mainly in association with severe hepatocellular injury, pancreatitis, and poor short-term outcomes; however, their occurrence during acute clinical deterioration associated with suspected post-transfusion hemolysis has not been specifically documented. The dog died three days after inclusion detection. This case expands the clinical settings in which blue-green leukocyte cytoplasmic inclusions may be encountered in dogs.

records.title: Case report: Long-term local control of recurrent lymphatic malformations using minocycline sclerotherapy following surgical resection in a dog.
records.abstract: Lymphatic malformation is a benign congenital vascular anomaly that is rarely reported in veterinary medicine. Complete surgical excision is extremely challenging because the boundary between the abnormal and normal tissues is poorly defined, which frequently results in recurrence. A 3-year-6-month-old castrated male mixed-breed dog (Chihuahua × Miniature Dachshund) presented with recurrent lymphatic malformations in the left inguinal and peripenile regions. The lesion had previously been surgically excised at another hospital but recurred shortly after surgery. Despite long-term prednisolone therapy, the lesion gradually enlarged, resulting in gait disturbance and decreased activity. Extensive surgical excision was performed at our hospital; however, early postoperative recurrence was observed. Repeat sclerotherapy with minocycline was subsequently administered for the recurrent cystic lesions. The large cystic lesions resolved or remained controlled after treatment, and long-term suppression of lesion progression was achieved. Although small residual lesions persisted, the dog maintained good activity and gait without marked progression at 535 days postoperatively. In addition, amplicon-based targeted deep sequencing of the PIK3CA hotspot regions did not identify any pathogenic variants. This case suggests that repeated minocycline sclerotherapy may represent a potential minimally invasive treatment option for canine lymphatic malformations that are difficult to control with surgical excision alone.

records.title: Non-Oliguric IRIS Grade V Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Suspected Leptospirosis in an Urban Dog Unvaccinated Against Leptospirosis from the Republic of Korea: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease that can cause severe acute kidney injury (AKI) in dogs. A three-year-old intact male Border Collie, unvaccinated against leptospirosis, with a history of exposure to urban stagnant water presented with acute vomiting, diarrhea, and moderate dehydration. Initial evaluation revealed extreme azotemia (blood urea nitrogen, 175.8 mg/dL; creatinine, 11.10 mg/dL) and hyperphosphatemia (13.6 mg/dL), consistent with International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) AKI Grade V; urine output remained within the non-oliguric range (2.15-3.0 mL/kg/h) throughout the catheterized period (Day 0-4). Clinical and imaging findings supported acute intrinsic renal injury over chronic kidney disease. A multiplex real-time PCR targeting the  Leptospira LipL32  gene was positive in urine (Ct 31.10), providing molecular evidence supporting active infection or shedding of pathogenic  Leptospira  spp., without identifying the infecting serovar. Empirical antimicrobial therapy targeting suspected leptospirosis, together with intravenous fluid therapy, was initiated on clinical suspicion prior to the PCR result. Renal and inflammatory biomarkers improved progressively over 22 days without extracorporeal kidney support; the patient's non-oliguric status, hemodynamic stability, and objective clinical improvement supported this management approach. This report documents, in detail, the clinicopathological recovery trajectory of a dog with non-oliguric IRIS Grade V AKI associated with suspected leptospirosis, information that may assist clinicians in recognizing and managing similarly severe presentations without assuming that dialysis is always required.

records.title: Resolution of Regenerative Anemia, Thrombocytopenia, and Syncope After Cytoreduction of an Infiltrative Angiolipoma in a Dog: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Angiolipomas are uncommon benign mesenchymal neoplasms composed of mature adipocytes and proliferating vascular channels. In dogs, infiltrative angiolipomas are rarely reported and have primarily been described as localized soft-tissue masses. An 11-year-old, 10.8 kg, castrated male Japanese Spitz was referred for evaluation of regenerative anemia, mild thrombocytopenia, recurrent syncopal episodes, and a 5-year history of a slowly enlarging ventral thoracic mass. Preoperative hematological evaluation demonstrated anemia with a hematocrit of 25.4% and an increased absolute reticulocyte count of 122.7 K/µL, supporting a regenerative erythropoietic response. The platelet count was mildly decreased at 109 × 10 3 /µL. D-dimer concentration was increased (737.61 ng/mL; reference interval, 0-250 ng/mL), whereas prothrombin time (9.5 s; reference interval, 5-15 s) and activated partial thromboplastin time (15.6 s; reference interval, 15-45 s) were within their reference intervals. Referral history indicated that previous infectious and immune-mediated evaluations had not identified a definitive cause, although the original external testing records were unavailable for verification. Computed tomography revealed a heterogeneous subcutaneous mass with mixed fat- and soft-tissue-attenuating components, suspected infiltration of the superficial pectoral muscle, and focal rather than diffuse contrast enhancement. Surgical cytoreduction, including partial myectomy, was performed because complete excision was not considered feasible owing to deep muscular infiltration. Histopathological examination confirmed an infiltrative angiolipoma characterized by mature adipocytes, numerous vascular channels, skeletal muscle infiltration, and frequent intravascular fibrin thrombi. Following surgery, the hematological abnormalities progressively improved without blood transfusion or long-term immunosuppressive therapy. The platelet count increased from 109 × 10 3 /µL preoperatively to 153 × 10 3 /µL by postoperative day 16 and 202 × 10 3 /µL by postoperative day 56. During the same period, the hematocrit increased from 25.4% to 45.0%, and the absolute reticulocyte count subsequently returned to the reference interval. The syncopal episodes ceased after surgery and did not recur during the available 12-month follow-up. Fibrinogen concentration and peripheral blood smear evaluation were unavailable, and serial postoperative coagulation testing was not performed. Accordingly, the temporal association between tumor cytoreduction and hematological improvement raises the possibility of a tumor-associated process, but neither the underlying mechanism nor a causal relationship could be established.

records.title: Rapid Clinical Improvement Temporally Associated with Off-Label LetiFend ®  Vaccination in Canine Leishmaniasis: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Canine leishmaniasis (CanL), caused by  Leishmania infantum , can be difficult to manage in dogs with severe clinical disease, particularly when established treatments are impractical or poorly tolerated. We report an approximately 3-year-old mixed-breed dog from Sardinia with clinically manifest CanL, anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked hyperglobulinemia, and an immunofluorescence antibody test titer of 1:4000. The dog's condition deteriorated during allopurinol treatment, with profound lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea, and complete refusal of food and water. Because escalation to combination leishmanicidal therapy (meglumine antimoniate or miltefosine) was considered clinically unsuitable in the severely debilitated patient, allopurinol monotherapy was discontinued after 18 days without clinical improvement, and one full commercial dose of the recombinant vaccine LetiFend ®  was administered subcutaneously off-label. No immediate adverse reaction was observed. Clinical improvement became apparent within approximately 10 days, and near-normal activity returned within three weeks. During follow-up, hematological parameters normalized and serum protein electrophoresis showed an increased albumin/globulin ratio and a reduced gamma-globulin fraction. Domperidone was subsequently introduced as long-term immunomodulatory follow-up, and allopurinol was temporarily reintroduced after transient laboratory deterioration in 2024; the dog remained clinically healthy through July 2026. The close temporal association is clinically noteworthy but cannot establish causality. This hypothesis-generating observation supports controlled investigation of therapeutic vaccination as a potential complementary approach in canine leishmaniasis.

records.title: Three-Dimensional Planning and Surgical Correction of Bilateral Developmental Valgus Deformity of the Manus in a Dog.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: A one-year-old, 48 kg, male neutered, Great Dane presented for bilateral thoracic limb lameness ascribed to an apparent developmental valgus deformity of both manus. Corrective radial-shaped osteotomies of the four weight-bearing metacarpal bones (II-V) were virtually planned based on CT scan data, and bone models of each corrected manus were three-dimensionally (3D)-printed, sterilized, and used intra-operatively to facilitate the procedure. In the right manus, metacarpal bones II, IV, and V were individually stabilized with bone plates and screws, while metacarpal bone III was stabilized with an intramedullary pin. Bone plates and screws were used to stabilize metacarpal bones II-V in the left manus. Postoperative alignment was deemed appropriate following both procedures. A caudally positioned splint was maintained for four weeks following each surgery, and all osteotomies obtained union within eight weeks of surgery. The dog was examined 79 weeks after the initial procedure and thoracic limb posture and gait were markedly improved. Virtual surgical planning (VSP) and printed bone models facilitated successful correction of this dog's deformities.

records.title: Salvage Surgery Including Rectal Wall Vas Deferens Pexy for Recurrent Bilateral Perineal Hernia with Bladder Retroflexion in a Dog: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Bladder retroflexion associated with perineal hernia may cause urinary dysfunction, and surgical correction can be challenging after repeated procedures because of extensive adhesions and altered anatomy. An 11-year-old, 7.5 kg, castrated male Pomeranian was referred for recurrent bilateral perineal hernia, bladder retroflexion, and persistent urinary dysfunction after multiple perineal and abdominal surgeries. A previous attempt at abdominal bladder reduction and cystopexy had failed because adhesions prevented adequate mobilization of the bladder. During salvage surgery, bilateral perineal adhesiolysis was performed first to release the displaced urinary tract structures, followed by an abdominal approach to restore the bladder to its normal intra-abdominal position. Modified bilateral vas deferens pexy was then performed by fixing the residual vasa deferentia to the rectal wall, and each side of the pelvic diaphragm was reconstructed according to the available tissues and defect configuration. Retrograde urethrocystography performed 8 days postoperatively demonstrated short-term anatomical correction, with restoration of the normal positions of the bladder, bladder neck, and urethra. Urinary function gradually improved but had not completely normalized by 150 days. Without further objective imaging, long-term mechanical stability and prevention of recurrence could not be established. This case describes a multimodal salvage strategy for recurrent bilateral perineal hernia with markedly altered anatomy after repeated surgery.

records.title: Clinical Course, Laboratory Findings, and Tissue Distribution of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus in a Naturally Infected Domestic Cat.
records.abstract: In June 2023, Poland experienced an unprecedented outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus infections in cats, raising concerns about the role of cats in HPAI H5N1 virus ecology and potential public health implications. We describe the clinical course and molecular findings in a cat designated as cat No. 14 during this outbreak, with emphasis on the viral load detected in various organs and tissues. The cat was initially examined for recurrent dermatological problems, although the owner also reported reduced activity. Over the following five days, the disease rapidly progressed, with systemic and neurological signs unresponsive to treatment. Blood analyses revealed no major haematological abnormalities, whereas serial serum biochemistry showed progressive abnormalities. Due to the poor prognosis, the cat was humanely euthanized five days after the initial veterinary examination. Tissue samples from major internal organs and lymph nodes, together with tracheal and rectal swabs and bile, were collected for real-time RT-PCR. Viral RNA was detected in all analysed samples except the intestines, mesenteric lymph nodes, rectal swab, and bile, with the highest viral loads observed in the cerebellum and brain. This case provides molecular evidence of widespread HPAI H5N1 viral RNA distribution across tissues, complemented by detailed haematological and biochemical findings, further characterizing the systemic nature of infection.
